title: Finite formal normalization for supplied parameter ideals
statement:
Let $(B,\mathfrak n)$ be a complete Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], let $e\geq0$, and consider either of the following cases. (a) $B$ is reduced, $\dim(B/\mathfrak q)=e$ for every minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], and $\Lambda\hookrightarrow B$ is a coefficient field inducing $\Lambda\cong B/\mathfrak n$; let $b_1,\ldots,b_e\in\mathfrak n$ satisfy $\sqrt{(b_1,\ldots,b_e)B}=\mathfrak n$. (b) $B$ is a domain of dimension $e+1$, $\Lambda$ is a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], and $\Lambda\hookrightarrow B$ is local and induces an isomorphism on residue fields; let $b_1,\ldots,b_e\in\mathfrak n$ satisfy $\sqrt{(\pi,b_1,\ldots,b_e)B}=\mathfrak n$. In either case the continuous evaluation map
$$\varphi:R=\Lambda[[T_1,\ldots,T_e]]\longrightarrow B,\qquad T_i\longmapsto b_i$$
[def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] is injective, local, induces an isomorphism on residue fields, and makes $B$ finite and torsion free as an $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. In case (a), writing $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $L_{\mathfrak q}=\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak q)$, the canonical map is an isomorphism $B\otimes_RK\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q\text{ minimal}}L_{\mathfrak q}$, and every $L_{\mathfrak q}/K$ is finite [def-weil-module-base-change].

Finiteness uses Tag 031D, lemma-finite-over-complete-ring; injectivity componentwise uses Tag 00OJ, lemma-integral-dim-up. Generic product is the reduced finite-dimensional algebra decomposition.

proof.text: Put $I=\mathfrak m_\Lambda R+(T_1,\ldots,T_e)$. A field and a DVR are Noetherian: all ideals are principal. The power-series Noetherian, domain, and local-ring statements therefore show that $R$ is a Noetherian local domain. The constant-coefficient quotient statement identifies $R/(T_1,\ldots,T_e)$ with $\Lambda$. Consequently the maximal ideal described by the local-ring statement is exactly $I$, and $R/I=\Lambda/\mathfrak m_\Lambda$. The complete-base power-series statement applied to $\Lambda$ and $\mathfrak m_\Lambda$ gives $I$-adic completeness, including for an arbitrary complete DVR, not just an unramified Cohen ring.

proof.text:
For $0\le i\le e$, the variable-quotient statement identifies $R/(T_1,\ldots,T_i)$ with $\Lambda[[T_{i+1},\ldots,T_e]]$, a Noetherian local domain by the three cited power-series statements. If $i<e$, the next variable is a nonzero element of its maximal ideal, so the nonzerodivisor dimension formula gives
$\dim R/(T_1,\ldots,T_i)=1+\dim R/(T_1,\ldots,T_{i+1})$.
Iterating yields $\dim R=e+\dim\Lambda$. A field has dimension zero. A DVR has dimension at most one by the maximal-ideal generator bound, and at least one from the prime chain $(0)\subsetneq(\pi)$. Thus $\dim R=e$ in (a) and $e+1$ in (b). This argument includes $e=0$, when there is no variable to remove.

proof.text: Apply the complete power-series universal property to the coefficient map $\Lambda\to B$, the ideal $\mathfrak n$, and the supplied $b_i\in\mathfrak n$. This constructs the evaluation map $\varphi$ with the prescribed values. Its image on $I$ is contained in $\mathfrak n$; hence $\varphi(I^m)\subseteq\mathfrak n^m$ proves continuity. The induced map $R/I\to B/\mathfrak n$ is the assumed coefficient residue-field isomorphism. Therefore an element outside $I$ has nonzero residue and its image is outside $\mathfrak n$; the inverse image of $\mathfrak n$ is exactly $I$, proving locality.

source.place: Tag 032D, lemma-complete-local-Noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular, parameter evaluation in Cases I and II; ILO IV 2.1.12 and IV 4.2.5

proof.text: Let $J=IB$, the supplied ideal $(b_1,\ldots,b_e)B$ in (a) or $(\pi,b_1,\ldots,b_e)B$ in (b). We use the given radical equality, not the existence of some other parameters. Choose generators $z_1,\ldots,z_s$ of $\mathfrak n$. Since $z_i\in\sqrt J$, choose $a_i\ge1$ with $z_i^{a_i}\in J$. Every monomial of degree $N=1+\sum_i(a_i-1)$ contains one such power, so $\mathfrak n^N\subseteq J\subseteq\mathfrak n$. This also covers $s=0$ by taking $N=1$. The quotient-Artinian-local statement applies to $B/J$. Its residue field is $k=R/I$, and the coefficient map gives an actual map $k\to B/J$: in (b) the uniformizer belongs to $J$. The Artinian finite-over-residue statement, applied to $k\to B/J$ and its one-dimensional residue quotient, shows $B/J$ finite over $k$. Finally $J^m\subseteq\mathfrak n^m$ gives $\bigcap_m I^mB=0$ by the assumed completeness of $B$. Together with the completeness of $R$ in Step 1, these are precisely the three hypotheses of the finite-over-complete-ring statement. It follows that $B$ is finite over $R$.

proof.text: Write $d=\dim R$. In (b) put $C=B$; in (a) fix any minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ and put $C=B/\mathfrak q$. In both cases $C$ is a nonzero finite $R$-module (images of generators of $B$ generate its quotient), and $\dim C=d$ by the hypotheses and Step 2. Suppose $0\ne f\in\ker(R\to C)$. This proper kernel lies in the maximal ideal of the local ring $R$, and $f$ is a nonzerodivisor since $R$ is a domain. Thus $\dim(R/(f))+1=d$ by the dimension formula. The same finite set generates $C$ over $R/(f)$, so finite-implies-integral and the integral dimension inequality give $d=\dim C\le\dim(R/(f))$, a contradiction. Hence $R\to C$ is injective. This proves injectivity in (b) and injectivity on every minimal component in (a), and therefore injectivity into $B$ in (a) as well. For $d=0$ the supposition is already impossible because the maximal ideal of $R=\Lambda$ is zero.

proof.text: In (b), if $0\ne r\in R$ and $rb=0$, injectivity and the domain property of $B$ imply $b=0$. In (a), Step 5 says that the image of $r$ in every $B/\mathfrak q$ is nonzero. The image of $r$ therefore lies in no minimal prime of $B$; the reduced-ring zero-divisor statement shows that multiplication by $r$ on $B$ is injective. Thus $B$ is torsion free over $R$ in either case.

proof.text: For the remaining assertions work in case (a), and set $S=R\setminus\{0\}$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. Identify the tensor product of the base-change definition with $S^{-1}B$ by $b\otimes(a/s)\mapsto ab/s$, with inverse $b/s\mapsto b\otimes(1/s)$; the balanced relations and the fraction equivalence relation verify these inverse maps. If $b_1',\ldots,b_h'$ generate $B$ over $R$, their images span this localization over $K$, so it is finite-dimensional. Let $t$ be any nonzerodivisor of $B$. If $tb/s=0$, some $u\in S$ has $utb=0$ in $B$, whence $ub=0$ and $b/s=0$. Multiplication by $t$ is therefore injective on $S^{-1}B$; on a finite-dimensional vector space an injective endomorphism is surjective, since it sends a basis to a linearly independent set of the same cardinality. In particular $tv=1$ for some $v$, so every such $t$ is invertible. Since Step 6 makes every element of $S$ a nonzerodivisor, the fraction maps in both directions identify $S^{-1}B$ with the total ring of fractions $Q(B)$.

source.place: Tag 02LX, lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points, total-fraction setting; elementary tensor/fraction calculation and finite-dimensional basis argument

proof.text: Apply the reduced Noetherian total-fraction statement to $B$. It gives finitely many minimal primes and the canonical isomorphism $Q(B)\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q}B_{\mathfrak q}$, with $B_{\mathfrak q}$ a field and $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}=0$. Thus $B\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ factors through $B/\mathfrak q$, and every nonzero class in this domain maps to a unit, since its representative is outside $\mathfrak q$. The induced map $\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak q)\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ and the localization map in the reverse direction both send a fraction $b/s$ to the same fraction, hence are inverse. Each $B/\mathfrak q$ is finite over $R$ and the map from $R$ is injective by Step 5, so the finite-domain-fraction-degree statement makes $L_{\mathfrak q}/K$ finite. Combining these maps with Step 7 gives the asserted isomorphism. All component maps send $b\otimes(a/s)$ to $a\bar b/\bar s$, so it is the canonical map in the statement.

Its clauses cover how the parent cohen-gabber-finite-presentations uses it in steps 3, 4 and 8. The cited statements give every claim the steps take from them. Step 1 builds R with maximal ideal I, Noetherian, local, a domain and complete, from the general power-series nodes. Step 2 gets dim R=e+dim Λ from quotient-variables, nonzerodivisor-dimension and the generator bound for a DVR. Step 3 uses the universal property with B 𝔫-adically complete, and locality comes from the residue isomorphism (π∈𝔫 because Λ→B is local). Step 4 replaces the old existential-parameters citation with a correct pigeonhole bound 𝔫^N⊆J from the supplied radical. It then checks Artinian quotient → finite over k → all three 031D hypotheses, with separatedness taken from the completeness definition. Step 5 proves injectivity on each component by the dimension contradiction through R/(f)→C integral. Step 6 gets torsion-freeness from the reduced zero-divisor criterion. Steps 7–8 prove the tensor ≅ S⁻¹B ≅ Q(B) ≅ ∏ Frac(B/𝔮) chain explicitly, with L_𝔮/K finite. Small cases checked: e=0 in both cases, k[[x,y]]/(xy) with t=x+y, and a ramified DVR.
